title: Coastal Dental: New Patient Special $79 (Meta ad live 1,624 days)
excerpt: Headline: "New Patient Special - Only $79! Contact Us Today!" Primary text: five trust bullets, including "sterilized office" and "family operated" (full text not reproduced by source).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a first dental visit to local families on the promise of a fixed $79 new-patient price because the practice is family operated and lists plain trust facts rather than claims.
structure.hook: A single price as the headline
structure.mechanism: none stated; trust facts substitute for mechanism
structure.big_idea: One price, five reasons to trust us
structure.voice_notes: Plain local-service register; no humor, no story.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 3276935695920103; start date March 24, 2022; 1,624 days running when verified live on September 3, 2026. Source cautions the long run likely reflects a small budget left on, not tested performance.

lessons: Local-service offer lead: price in the headline, trust facts as bullets, literal CTA.
Longevity is a weak proxy when spend is small; record budget caveats with the start date.
notes: Ad text available only as excerpts on the source page; Library ID recorded for direct verification.

title: Umi: Learn a language from 0 to fluency in 1 year by watching TV clips (625 days)
excerpt: Primary text opens: "Learn a language from 0 to fluency in 1 year, by watching TV clips." Headline: "Want be fluent in Japanese in 1 Year?" (typo is in the ad). CTA: Download.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a language app to would-be Japanese learners on the promise of fluency in one year because the method is watching TV clips, a mechanism the reader already enjoys.
structure.hook: Result (fluency), timeframe (1 year), mechanism (TV clips) in one line
structure.voice_notes: Direct, promise-first; first frame shows the product in use on a phone with the promise as caption.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 897899378791711; start December 17, 2024; 625 days running as of September 3, 2026 (no versions flag). Source notes the run shows continued spend, not proven results.

lessons: Promise lead for solution-aware traffic: desire, timeframe and named mechanism in the first line.
A typo survived 600+ days; polish is not what the market buys.

title: Dot & Key niacinamide serum: seven emoji bullets of benefits and proof (492 days)
excerpt: Primary text: seven emoji bullets listing three benefits and four proof points, including "Clinically Proven." Image carries one product and one number (full text not reproduced by source).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a niacinamide serum to skincare buyers on the promise of visible brightening because the ad stacks clinical and ingredient proof points behind each benefit.
structure.hook: Product plus one number in the image; claims in the text
structure.voice_notes: Bullet list with emoji markers; benefit then proof.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 1742086950046918; start April 29, 2025; 492 days running as of September 3, 2026 (multiple versions).

lessons: Split the job: image carries product and the one number, text carries the claims and proof.
Versioned ads run long because bullets can be rewritten per launch while the frame stays.
notes: "Clinically Proven" appears without a cited study on the source page; a ledger would require the study ID.

title: Consumer Reports: Don't Buy Without Checking Consumer Reports (mattress ratings, 183 days)
excerpt: Headline: "Don't Buy Without Checking Consumer Reports". Primary text names three mattresses it rates. CTA: Subscribe.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a ratings subscription to people about to buy a mattress on the promise of not making an expensive mistake because the ad names the exact brands it has tested.
structure.hook: Naming competitors' products the reader is already comparing
structure.voice_notes: Warning register; promises an answer, sells the answer.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 1584467826181628; start March 4, 2026; 183 days running as of September 3, 2026; this creative and text appear in 4 ads.

lessons: Intercept the decision moment: name the specific products the buyer is weighing.
An information product can be sold as loss avoidance on a big purchase.

title: Factor: up to 50g protein, no more stressing about protein (175 days)
excerpt: Primary text highlights "up to 50g" of protein and "no more stressing about protein." 27-second video labelled against "Every Other Meal Kit"; headline offers 50 percent off the first box.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells prepared meals to protein-tracking eaters on the promise of hitting protein targets without effort because each meal carries up to 50g, a specification competitors do not lead with.
structure.hook: One specification against the category
structure.big_idea: Us vs every other meal kit on one number
structure.voice_notes: Product-photo-with-motion; comparison label does the arguing.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 947487921506032; start March 12, 2026; 175 days running as of September 3, 2026 (multiple versions).

lessons: Stage-4 market: one specification, framed against the whole category, is the differentiator.
The discount is the headline field, not the hook.

title: HOKA: The legs give out. The heart doesn't. (155 days)
excerpt: Primary text: "The legs give out. The heart doesn't. Together We Fly Higher." No headline; CTA is a menu rather than a button.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells HOKA to runners who already know the brand on a feeling of endurance because identification, not an offer, is the only move left at stage five.
structure.hook: Aphorism about effort
structure.voice_notes: Brand register; no product name, no offer.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 1279489107485101; start April 1, 2026; 155 days running as of September 3, 2026; 3 ads use this creative and text. Source notes it works only because the brand is already known.

lessons: Anti-pattern for a DR brief: no proof, no offer, no CTA works only for an established brand; the rubric should penalize this for unknown advertisers.
Stage-5 identification copy is an edge case, not a template.
notes: Included as a negative example for retrieval contrast.

title: Solawave: OUR BIGGEST SALE EVER, LIVE NOW / BUY 1 GET 1 FREE (139 days)
excerpt: Primary text opens "OUR BIGGEST SALE EVER, LIVE NOW," claiming the biggest sale and that the device works. Headline in image: "BUY 1 GET 1 FREE". CTA: Shop Now (a second "Shop Offer" button is drawn into the image).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells an LED face mask to shoppers who have seen it before on the promise of two for one because the sale is framed as the biggest the brand has run.
structure.hook: Sale announcement in caps
structure.voice_notes: Promotional caps; person using product at top, offer as largest text, fake button last in eye path.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 2010645566183162; start April 17, 2026; 139 days running as of September 3, 2026 (no versions flag).

lessons: Offer lead for product-aware traffic: deal in line one, product in use, button restated in the image.
A 'biggest sale ever' that runs 139 days is a deadline without a mechanism; flag for the factual review.

title: Zocdoc: Putting off that cleaning because you dread the phone tag? (91 days)
excerpt: Primary text opens with the objection: "Putting off that cleaning because you dread the phone tag and the 'is this covered?' talk?" CTA: Book Now.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells online dentist booking to people avoiding a cleaning on the promise of skipping phone tag and insurance confusion because the app answers both in three beats.
structure.hook: The reader's own excuse, in their words
structure.big_idea: The reason you're putting it off is the thing we remove
structure.voice_notes: Conversational objection-first; video and text target different objections for the same answer.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 4163899043741831; start June 4, 2026; 91 days running as of September 3, 2026 (multiple versions).

lessons: Problem-aware lead that names the need in the reader's words without 'Are you tired of'.
Run variants where video and text each carry a different objection.

title: KURU Footwear: zombie-movie setup, foot pain is the real casualty (59 days)
excerpt: Primary text opens with a zombie-movie setup and says the shoes make foot pain "the real casualty." Description: "Over 3M Pairs Sold".

structure.argument_sentence: This sells supportive shoes to people with heel pain on the promise of pain relief because three million pairs sold and plain review, shipping and return facts back it.
structure.hook: Borrowed genre (zombie film) for the first seconds
structure.big_idea: Foot pain is the real casualty
structure.voice_notes: Entertaining hook, then plain proof does the selling.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 1339489931715040; start July 6, 2026; 59 days running as of September 3, 2026 (multiple versions).

lessons: Attention device and proof are separate jobs; the hook borrows a genre, the body uses counts and policies.
Social-proof count ('3M pairs') belongs in the description field where the skim path lands.

title: Nectar Sleep: You could spend $4,000+ on a pricey mattress bundle. But why would you?
excerpt: Primary text: "You could spend $4,000+ on a pricey mattress bundle. But why would you?" Headline: "NOW Start The 365-Night Trial".

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a mattress and adjustable base to comparison shoppers on the promise of the same bundle for far less because the risk is carried by a 365-night trial.
structure.hook: Price anchor against the expensive alternative, then a question
structure.big_idea: Same bundle, a fraction of $4,000, a year to decide
structure.voice_notes: Rhetorical question lead; feature bullets follow.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 1073276592055585; start August 20, 2026; only 14 days running when verified September 3, 2026. Too new for longevity to mean anything.

lessons: Anchor first, then offer the risk reversal as the headline rather than the price.
Record young ads separately from proven ones; do not let the retrieval layer treat 14 days as a control.
notes: Included for the anchor-then-trial structure; performance unknown.

title: Ling: Can't find your language on Duolingo? Learn languages with Ling instead!
excerpt: Primary text: "Can't find your language on Duolingo? Learn languages with Ling instead!" Headline: five star emoji and "Try Now". Caption in video: "I'm not an AI".

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a language app to learners the market leader does not serve on the promise that their language is here because Ling positions itself only against the gap in Duolingo's catalog.
structure.hook: Competitor-conditional question
structure.voice_notes: Real person on camera, caption establishes the speaker is human.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 924573780049552; start August 12, 2026; 22 days running as of September 3, 2026.

lessons: Stage-4 positioning: define the product by the leader's gap rather than by a bigger claim.
'I'm not an AI' is a candor device for 2026 social; note it as a dated trust marker.
notes: Performance unknown; structure only.

title: HelloFresh: free breakfast for life / Get 10 free meals
excerpt: Primary text includes "free breakfast for life." Headline: "Get 10 free meals". CTA: Sign Up. Creator-style hook delivered from the brand account.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a meal-kit subscription to people who know the category on the promise of ten free meals and free breakfast for life because the offer, not the food, is the news.
structure.hook: Creator-style delivery of a brand offer
structure.big_idea: Free meals to start, free breakfast forever
structure.voice_notes: UGC register from a brand account.

results.detail: Meta Ad Library ID 912167651413741; start August 11, 2026; 23 days running as of September 3, 2026. Source treats it as a test in progress.

lessons: Offer lead for a saturated category: stack the bonus in the headline field and keep the primary text as a creator hook.
'For life' bonus copy needs a ledger entry for the terms.
notes: Performance unknown.

title: AdEspresso $1,000 copy-length experiment (Custom Audiences eBook lead magnet)
author_or_company: AdEspresso (Paul Fairbrother; copy by Ana Gotter)
excerpt: Seven ad texts for the same eBook offer, from one sentence to six paragraphs, identical image, headline, link description and CTA. Ad copy appears only as images on the source page and is not reproduced here.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a free Custom Audiences guide to Facebook advertisers on the promise of better targeting because the longer versions explain what the guide covers before asking for the click.
structure.hook: unknown (copy in images)
structure.voice_notes: Professional copywriter; test held creative constant.

results.detail: $1,000 over 14 days, about $142.90 per ad, 1% US lookalike (about 2.1M people), one ad per ad set, optimized for conversions. Stated: "The trend that we observed is that the mid to long ad text produced the lowest CPA and the maximum number of leads." One-sentence and emoji-bullet versions had "significantly higher" CPA; "Poorly performing ad text costs 2.4 times per lead than the best version." Campaign CPC about $5, CPM about $46, 79% landing conversion rate. 135 marketers polled: 89% voted for the three worst versions.

losing_variants.result: Significantly higher cost per lead; among the three worst

lessons: For a B2B lead magnet to cold lookalikes, mid-to-long primary text beat one-liners by up to 2.4x on cost per lead.
Marketer intuition favored short copy and was wrong 89% of the time; the rubric should not reward brevity by default.
Hold image, headline and CTA constant when testing text length.
notes: Per-variant CTR and CPA are in charts not available as text; winner not named individually.

title: Strategyzer event tickets: copy rewrite takes campaign from 1 purchase to 92 (AdEspresso / AOK Marketing / Sarah Sal)
author_or_company: Sarah Sal (AOK Marketing) for Strategyzer, reported by AdEspresso
excerpt: Revised ad used storytelling copy that previewed what attendees would learn (original and revised ads shown only as images on the source; text not reproduced).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a Strategyzer event to business-model practitioners on the promise of specific takeaways because the copy previews the content as a story rather than announcing the event.
structure.hook: Story preview of what attendees will learn
structure.big_idea: Show the lesson, not the event
structure.voice_notes: Narrative, longer, educational.

results.detail: Original campaign spent $4,433.53 over about three weeks for 1 sale. Revised copy "took the event from 1 purchase to 92, with an average CPA of $123.45"; source calls it "a 96.72% decrease in cost from changing the copy alone." Reported by the agency and AdEspresso, not an independent split test.

losing_variants.description: Original announcement-style ad (audience and image tested first)

lessons: Changing argument and tone outperformed changing audience and image; copy is the higher-order variable.
For an event, preview the content as story and specifics instead of announcing the date.
notes: Vendor-reported; original and revised copy not legible in source text.

title: Scoro: 'Sign Up' CTA beats 'Learn More' by 14.5% (AdEspresso test)
author_or_company: Scoro, test by AdEspresso (reported via Advertisemint)
excerpt: Same ad, two CTA buttons: "Sign Up" vs "Learn More". Ad copy not reproduced by the source.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a SaaS trial to teams on the promise stated in the ad because the button names the exact action the ad asks for.
structure.hook: unknown
structure.voice_notes: unknown

results.detail: "Sign Up" CTA outperformed "Learn More" by 14.5% (metric not specified by the secondary source; original attributed to AdEspresso's '5 Facebook Ads Split Tests with Game-Changing Results'). Secondary source notes some of its cited tests fall short of 10,000 impressions / 500 clicks.

lessons: The literal CTA (the action the ad wants) beat the soft CTA; matches the standard's 'one literal CTA'.
notes: Secondary report; original AdEspresso post not fetched. Sample size caveat stated by source.

title: Exclamation mark removed: CTR 2.32% vs 1.10% (AdEspresso test)
author_or_company: AdEspresso (advertiser not named), reported via Advertisemint
excerpt: Same copy with and without a closing exclamation mark (copy not reproduced by source).

structure.argument_sentence: unknown; the test isolates punctuation only.
structure.hook: unknown
structure.voice_notes: Version without exclamation mark read as less salesy.

results.detail: CTR 2.32% without exclamation mark vs 1.10% with; source also claims 187% better cost per click for the version without. Attributed to AdEspresso.

losing_variants.description: Same copy ending in an exclamation mark

lessons: One data point against reflexive exclamation marks in primary text; consistent with the tell detector treating them at human rates, not as hype markers.
notes: Single secondary report; advertiser and sample size unknown.

title: Scoro: flag emoji in headline, CTR 0.846% vs 0.351% (AdEspresso test)
author_or_company: Scoro, test by AdEspresso (reported via Advertisemint)
excerpt: Identical text, images and CTA; one headline carries a flag emoji, the other does not (copy not reproduced by source).

structure.argument_sentence: unknown; the test isolates a headline emoji.
structure.hook: Country flag emoji signalling local relevance
structure.voice_notes: unknown

results.detail: CTR 0.846% with emoji vs 0.351% without (about 2.4x). Attributed to AdEspresso.

losing_variants.description: Same headline without the flag emoji

lessons: A geographic marker in the headline field can double CTR for geo-targeted B2B; the gain is relevance, not decoration.
notes: Low absolute CTRs; secondary report.

title: Dollar Shave Club: Our Blades Are F***ing Great (launch video, March 6, 2012)
excerpt: Title: "DollarShaveClub.com - Our Blades Are F***ing Great". CEO Michael Dubin delivers the pitch "in a nonchalant and sarcastic manner" (opening line not captured from a fetched source).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a $1-a-month razor subscription to men annoyed at razor prices on the promise that the blades are good enough because the founder says so to camera while mocking the category's over-engineering.
structure.hook: Founder on camera, profane product claim in the title
structure.big_idea: Stop paying for shave tech you don't need
structure.close: join the club at the URL
structure.voice_notes: Deadpan founder monologue; humor as proof of confidence.

results.detail: Video "prompted 12,000 orders in a two-day span after it was released"; server overwhelmed within the first hour; over 27 million views as of November 2020; Ad Age Viral Video Award 2012 "Best Out-of-Nowhere Video Campaign". Cited to LA Times (Aug 16, 2013) and NYT (Apr 11, 2013).

lessons: A founder as narrator who exists is the strongest form of the 'narrator exists' rule.
Category critique plus a price anchor can carry a cold launch with no testimonials.
notes: Script not stored; YouTube fetch blocked. Wikipedia cross-checked via the Michael Dubin article (same figures).

title: Squatty Potty: the pooping unicorn (Harmon Brothers, October 2015)
funnel_position: cold to online purchase and retail lift
excerpt: A unicorn puppet releasing colorful soft-serve ice cream, narrated by a Prince Charming figure who explains elimination posture; the source describes the approach as "edutainment" (script lines not quoted by source).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a toilet footstool to people who never thought about posture on the promise of easier, more complete elimination because squatting straightens the colon, shown with a unicorn and ice cream instead of the real thing.
structure.hook: Absurd visual metaphor for an unmentionable
structure.mechanism: squat posture unkinks the colon (puborectalis explanation)
structure.voice_notes: Fairy-tale narrator; mechanism taught in full before the product; humor lowers the taboo.

results.detail: Company-reported: from the October 2015 debut to end of January 2016 online sales up 600 percent and retail sales up 200 percent; CEO Bobby Edwards: "We had estimated sales of $12 million last year. We reached $18 million." 2016 goal $25 million. Wikipedia (citing The Guardian) states the ad "went viral and increased sales" and more than five million units sold lifetime.

lessons: Unaware market: teach the mechanism inside a story before naming the product.
A metaphor that keeps the taboo at arm's length makes the ad shareable; sharing is the distribution mechanism.
notes: Sales figures are company statements and overlap with Shark Tank exposure. Opening line not captured.

title: Keto Chow: What would happen if the witch from Hansel and Gretel ate Keto Chow instead of kids? (Harmon Brothers, 2018)
excerpt: Premise as stated: "What would happen if the witch from Hansel and Gretel ate Keto Chow instead of kids?" Second campaign (2020): a prince who could not lose weight until he used Keto Chow.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a keto meal shake to dieters who know keto on the promise of an easy complete keto meal because a fairy-tale frame makes the comparison to other shakes entertaining.
structure.hook: Fairy-tale character with a dietary twist
structure.mechanism: complete keto nutrition in a shake
structure.voice_notes: Harmon Brothers comedic spokesperson format.

results.detail: Agency-reported: "In a single year Keto Chow went from hundreds of thousands to several millions in revenue"; co-founder Chris Bair: "Three months after we launched the first ad, our revenue increased 121%." Second campaign: "In less than six months from the release of that campaign Keto Chow brought in an additional $7.1M." Now "eight figures in annual revenue."

lessons: A story lead can serve a solution-aware market when the story's twist is the product's category.
Agency case figures are self-reported; store as such.
notes: No script beyond the premise line.

title: GoTREADS: stuck-in-the-mud Sprint campaign (Harmon Brothers, December 2020)
excerpt: Spokesperson-driven ad with "stuck in the mud" wordplay and a dad joke; "video proof that the GoTREADS product can rescue ANY car from being stuck— even a firetruck!" (script not reproduced).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells traction boards to drivers who have been stuck on the promise of getting any vehicle out because the ad shows it rescuing a firetruck.
structure.hook: Comedic spokesperson on a familiar frustration
structure.big_idea: If it can free a firetruck it can free you
structure.voice_notes: Lower-budget 'Sprint' format: less fantastical spokesperson, funny edge.

results.detail: Agency-reported: "Half of GoTREADS' 2020 sales came in December, the month the campaign launched"; first ten days of January 2021 brought 20% of the previous year's revenue; met 5-year goal 5 months after release; "less than one year after launching, GoTREADS grew 4,300%."

lessons: Demonstration at an extreme (firetruck) is the proof for a physical product; claim never exceeds what is shown.
Documented pivot from trade shows to video plus ecommerce; results are self-reported.

title: Skull Shaver: Beast Trimmer video ads, CPC down 40%, wholesale orders tripled (Harmon Brothers)
funnel_position: paid social to ecommerce and wholesale
excerpt: Case study headline: "THE CAMPAIGN PAID FOR ITSELF". Skull Shaver VP Peter Gold: "We immediately saw a jump in revenue, and within two months the creative had paid for itself." (script not described).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells an ergonomic head shaver to men who shave their heads on the promise of a faster, closer shave because the video demonstrates the device (details not in source).
structure.hook: unknown
structure.voice_notes: unknown

results.detail: Agency-reported: "reduced their Cost Per Click, tripled wholesale orders, and supercharged online sales in two months"; image label "40% reduction of CPC"; agency homepage adds "over 100 Million views in 3 months." Context: post iOS 14.5 paid social.

lessons: Record the metric the client chose (CPC) and what it does not show (conversion); a results field should name the metric.
notes: Structure largely unknown; included for results documentation only.

title: Dr. Squatch: You're not a dish. You're a man. (Raindrop, 3-minute explainer)
excerpt: Case study title: "You're not a dish. You're a man." A 3-minute social explainer starring comedian James Schrader, described by the agency as "edutainment" (script not reproduced).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells natural bar soap to men who use whatever is in the shower on the promise of better skin and smell because mass-market body wash is detergent made for dishes, not men.
structure.hook: Reframe of the current product as detergent
structure.mechanism: natural cold-process soap vs chemical detergent
structure.voice_notes: Comedic spokesman, mechanism-first, long for social (3 minutes).

results.detail: Agency-reported: more than 120 million views and 100,000 shares across YouTube and Facebook; No. 1 on YouTube's 2020 TrueView for Action Advertising Leaderboard; partnership began 2017 and the agency says it "helped grow sales 30X to over $100M in annual revenue" (not attributed to this video alone). CEO quote cites "over 300 million views" for the body of work.

lessons: Unaware market: open by renaming the reader's current solution, then teach the mechanism.
Three minutes works on social when the mechanism is the entertainment.
notes: View figures conflict within the source (120M vs 300M); recorded both.

title: Old Spice: The Man Your Man Could Smell Like (Wieden+Kennedy, February 2010)
excerpt: Campaign title: "The Man Your Man Could Smell Like"; single-take monologue addressed to women about their men (opening line not captured from a fetched source).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells men's body wash to the women who buy it on the promise that their man could smell like this man because the spokesman addresses her directly and absurdly.
structure.hook: Direct address to the buyer, not the user
structure.voice_notes: Hyper-confident deadpan monologue; one unbroken shot.

results.detail: Online release February 4, 2010; TV February 8, 2010. Over 11 million online views by end of June 2010; 8 of the top 11 most-popular YouTube videos mid-July 2010 (Adweek); over 60 million views as of February 22, 2022; Cannes Lions Grand Prix for Film June 2010; Primetime Emmy nomination/win for Outstanding Commercial 2010; 2011 Gold Cannes Lion for Creative Effectiveness (Old Spice article). 186 personalized response videos filmed over two and a half days. Sales percentages not given in the fetched sources.

lessons: Address the purchaser rather than the user when they differ.
Response videos turned a spot into a two-way campaign; distribution mechanics are part of the ad.
notes: Widely cited 107% sales lift was not present in any fetched source and is omitted.

title: Blendtec: Will It Blend? (series from October 30, 2006)
funnel_position: brand demonstration to retail and online
excerpt: Opening line: "Will it blend? That is the question." Closing caption: "Yes, it blends!" Format: Tom Dickson blends an unlikely object (iPhone, marbles, golf balls), slow-motion replay, examines the result.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a $400 blender to kitchen buyers on the promise that it will blend anything because the founder blends an iPhone on camera.
structure.hook: A question the viewer wants answered
structure.mechanism: motor power demonstrated by extreme objects
structure.voice_notes: Lab-coat deadpan; identical structure every episode.

results.detail: Series ran October 30, 2006 to November 10, 2020. September 2007: videos earned about $15,000 from host Revver (USA Today). Nominated 2007 YouTube Award Best Series; Net magazine 2007 Viral Video Campaign of the Year; bronze Clio 2008 (citation needed per source). Sales lift figures not present in fetched sources.

lessons: Pure demonstration proof: the claim is the demonstration, the strongest C9 score.
A repeatable format with one question is a 14-year control.
notes: The often-quoted 700% sales increase was not found in fetched sources and is omitted.

title: Poo-Pourri: Girls Don't Poop (2013)
excerpt: Title: "Girls Don't Poop". A prim British-accented woman on a toilet explains the product (opening line not captured from a fetched source).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a before-you-go toilet spray to women on the promise of no one knowing because an elegant narrator says the unsayable and explains the oil-film mechanism.
structure.hook: Elegant woman, unmentionable subject
structure.mechanism: essential-oil film traps odor below the water
structure.voice_notes: Refined register colliding with crude subject; mechanism explained in plain terms.

results.detail: Video "seen more than 31 million times"; USA Today named it one of 2013's worst advertisements. Company: over 17 million bottles sold by January 2016, $300 million valuation 2016, over 60 million bottles and 350 million combined video views by May 2019 (company-level, not video-specific).

lessons: Critics' 'worst ad' lists and sales results diverge; the rubric should predict beat/lose, not taste.
Unaware market handled by a narrator who exists and a mechanism stated in one sentence.

title: Peloton: The Gift That Gives Back (November 2019) - documented loser
excerpt: A husband gives his wife a Peloton for Christmas; after a year of riding she says she "didn't realize how much this would change me." Played by Monica Ruiz.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a Peloton as a gift to spouses on the promise of a transformed partner because a year of vlogged rides shows the change.
structure.hook: Surprise gift reveal
structure.voice_notes: Earnest vlog-diary; read by viewers as implying the husband wanted her thinner.

results.detail: The Guardian (Dec 4, 2019): "Peloton loses $1.5bn in value over 'dystopian, sexist' exercise bike ad." Peloton defended it as celebrating a "fitness and wellness journey" (Ad Age, Dec 3, 2019). Aviation Gin hired the actress for a spoof, "The Gift That Doesn't Give Back" (CNN, Dec 7, 2019).

losing_variants.description: The ad itself is the loser: an already-fit wife receiving exercise equipment from her husband

lessons: Market-first failure: the premise insulted the buyer segment; no line-level fix repairs a wrong-premise story.
Cold-read the story for the implied accusation about the reader before polishing.
notes: Stock move is correlation reported by press; recorded as stated.

title: Tai Lopez: Here in my garage (67 Steps YouTube pre-roll, c. 2015)
excerpt: Pre-roll filmed in a garage with a Lamborghini; the ad "extolled the virtues of knowledge over materialism while also showing off his Lamborghini" (opening line not captured from a fetched source).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a $67-a-month success course to young men wanting money on the promise that reading and knowledge got the speaker his cars because the proof is parked behind him.
structure.hook: Luxury car plus a contradiction (books matter more)
structure.big_idea: Knowledge over things, said in front of the things
structure.voice_notes: Casual direct-to-camera; the car does the proving.

results.detail: Source states the ad "became viral" and "prompted parodies and spoofs" (VICE, Sept 14, 2015; Intelligencer, Oct 6, 2025); no views, spend or sales figures given. Course criticized for not allowing cancellations and for upselling.

lessons: Implied-income proof via lifestyle display is the pattern the standard forbids (effortless-income claims); keep as a negative exemplar.
Ubiquity is not evidence; record 'viral' as none when no figure is stated.
notes: Included as a compliance anti-pattern.

title: Sherwin Cody School: Do You Make These Mistakes in English? (ran 40+ years)
author_or_company: Sherwin Cody with Maxwell Sackheim (Ruthrauff and Ryan); later managed by Victor Schwab
excerpt: Headline: "Do You Make These Mistakes in English?" Lead paragraph gives class-conscious examples of mistakes and ends that many people "show themselves lacking in the essential points of English" "Every time they talk or write."

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a home-study English course to ambitious adults on the promise of never being judged for their speech because the ad shows the exact mistakes they make and offers a free test by mail.
structure.hook: A question that makes the reader check themselves
structure.mechanism: Cody's 100% self-correcting method (coupon for free book)
structure.big_idea: Your English is being judged every time you speak
structure.close: mail the coupon for the free book
structure.voice_notes: Plain, slightly stern; examples carry the shame.

results.detail: Campaign ran "more than 40 years" in pulp and slick magazines, comics and newspapers; course bought by over 150,000 students from 1918. Schwab's ten-year comparison found response "near three times better" than the alternative headline "How to Speak and Write Masterly English" (Schwab, Printers' Ink Monthly, Sept 1939; NYT, July 16, 1956).

losing_variants.description: Headline "How to Speak and Write Masterly English"
losing_variants.result: About one-third the response of the question headline over ten years of testing

lessons: A problem-aware question headline beat a promise headline ~3:1 over a decade; the headline named the reader's fear, not the course.
Longevity as control: unchanged for 40 years because it kept winning tests.
notes: Pre-1929 US ad, public domain. Full text not captured from a fetched source; Battistella (OUP 2008) p. 39 reproduces it.

title: Listerine: chronic halitosis campaign (1920s)
excerpt: Ads "featured forlorn young women and men, eager for marriage but turned off by their mate's rotten breath." One quoted line: "Can I be happy with him in spite of that?"

structure.argument_sentence: This sells an antiseptic rinse to single adults on the promise of marriageability because it names a medical-sounding condition (halitosis) nobody will tell you that you have.
structure.hook: A romantic failure with an unspoken cause
structure.big_idea: You may have halitosis and no one will tell you
structure.voice_notes: Story vignette, clinical term as the turn.

results.detail: Per Freakonomics (Levitt & Dubner, 2009, p. 87), cited by Wikipedia: "In just seven years, the company's revenues rose from $115,000 to more than $8 million." Twitchell: "Listerine did not make mouthwash as much as it made halitosis."

lessons: Unaware market created by naming the problem; story lead with the mechanism word as the pivot.
The problem-invention pattern is the one the modern factual review must flag (manufactured condition).
notes: The 'Often a bridesmaid but never a bride' headline was not found in fetched sources and is not quoted. Pre-1929 ads are public domain; the specific 1925 ad text was not captured.

title: Odorono: sweating as embarrassment (1919 strategy; 'Within the Curve of a Woman's Arm')
author_or_company: Odorono (Edna Murphey) / J. Walter Thompson (James Webb Young)
excerpt: Sub-head as quoted: "A frank discussion of a subject too often avoided." Strategy (1919, Ladies' Home Journal): portray perspiration as a social embarrassment rather than a hygiene matter.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells an antiperspirant to women who did not think they had a problem on the promise of never offending because the ad frankly says others notice and will not tell you.
structure.hook: A frank discussion of what no one mentions
structure.voice_notes: Editorial, confiding, slightly shaming.

results.detail: Wikipedia (Edna Murphey): in 1919, after Odorono switched to portraying sweating as an embarrassing problem, sales rose 112 percent (no inline citation given). The 'Within the Curve' headline is cited to Better Homes and Gardens, June 1935, p. 171, a later run.

losing_variants.result: Slower sales; the shift to social embarrassment produced the 112% rise, per source

lessons: The same product sold twice as fast when the ad changed the problem from hygiene to social judgment: market and desire above mechanism.
Candor ('frank discussion') as a lead device for taboo categories.
notes: 1919 ad is public domain; 1935 reprint text is not. Full text not captured.

title: U.S. School of Music: They Laughed When I Sat Down at the Piano But When I Started to Play! (1926)
author_or_company: John Caples for U.S. School of Music (Ruthrauff and Ryan)
funnel_position: cold print to coupon for free book
excerpt: Headline: "They Laughed When I Sat Down at the Piano But When I Started to Play!" First-person story of a party guest who surprises the room; coupon for a free book (body text not captured from fetched sources).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells mail-order piano lessons to adults who wish they could play on the promise of the room's admiration because a first-person narrator shows the moment the laughter turns.
structure.hook: Open loop in the headline (laughed... but when)
structure.mechanism: learn at home without a teacher (print-and-picture lessons)
structure.big_idea: The revenge of the quiet one
structure.close: mail the coupon for the free book and demonstration lesson
structure.voice_notes: First-person narrative, dialogue, party scene; long copy.

results.detail: Wikipedia (citing White 1971): the ad was "highly successful" and is "considered one of the 100 greatest advertisements of all time." swiped.co lists it as "Ran 1927" and "Quite possibly the most swiped advertisement ever." No response figures in fetched sources.

lessons: Story lead with the payoff withheld in the headline; the ad is itself a testimonial scene (note: a fictional narrator, forbidden under the modern standard).
Order-form question ('do you have an instrument') qualified the lead for the back-end sale.
notes: Public domain (1926). Full text not captured; secondary source https://swiped.co/file/they-laughed-when-i-sat-down-at-the-piano-by-john-caples/ shows the headline only.

title: Volkswagen: Think small. (DDB, 1959)
author_or_company: Volkswagen of America / Doyle Dane Bernbach (Julian Koenig, Helmut Krone)
excerpt: Headline: "Think small." Mostly white space with a small image of the Beetle; body copy lists the advantages of owning a small car.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a small German car to Americans trained to want big ones on the promise of practical advantages because the ad admits the car is small and argues from that fact.
structure.hook: Two-word contrarian imperative
structure.mechanism: small car: parking, fuel, insurance, repairs
structure.voice_notes: Dry, honest, self-deprecating; sans-serif, black and white.

results.detail: Advertising Age (Garfield, March 29, 1999) ranked it the best advertising campaign of the 20th century; the Wikipedia article gives no sales figures.

lessons: Candor against the category's idea (C8 differentiation at level 3: the opposite of the category idea).
Recognition is not a result; store as none when no figure exists.

title: Rolls-Royce: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in the new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock (Ogilvy, 1958)
author_or_company: David Ogilvy / Ogilvy, Benson & Mather for Rolls-Royce
excerpt: Headline: "At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in the new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock". Body: numbered factual points about the car (body text not reproduced by the source page).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a Rolls-Royce to wealthy Americans on the promise of engineering quality because a technical editor's specific observation stands in for every adjective.
structure.hook: A specific, verifiable detail quoted from a motor magazine
structure.big_idea: Quiet is the proof of quality
structure.voice_notes: Factual, long, editorial; no superlatives.

results.detail: Source: ran 1958-1962; Ogilvy tested 26 headlines with colleagues before choosing; "Rolls-Royce sales in 1958 rose 50 percent over 1957" (figure from Ogilvy's own account, not independently verified by the source).

losing_variants.result: Rejected in favor of the clock line; no public data

lessons: Headline precision matches evidence: a quoted observation beats a claim.
Long factual body copy for an expensive purchase.
notes: A 1933 Pierce-Arrow ad used a near-identical line (per source).

title: Avis: We Try Harder Because We're Number 2 (DDB, 1962)
author_or_company: Avis / Doyle Dane Bernbach (Paula Green credited with the line)
excerpt: Line: "We Try Harder Because We're Number 2" (DDB article). Motto adopted 1962 under CEO Robert Townsend (Avis article).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells Avis rentals to business travellers on the promise of better service because an admitted second place is the reason the staff cannot afford to be careless.
structure.hook: Admission of being number two
structure.mechanism: underdog effort: clean ashtrays, full tanks (service specifics)
structure.voice_notes: Candid, short, declarative.

results.detail: Slogan used about 50 years until the 2012 rebrand to "It's Your Space" (CNBC 2012, via Avis article). Profit/loss and market-share figures not present in fetched sources.

lessons: Candor as positioning: name the weakness and make it the reason for the benefit.
Fifty-year longevity recorded; the oft-cited turnaround figures were not found and are omitted.
notes: Two Wikipedia sources used; DDB article for the line, Avis article for adoption and duration.

title: Dickie Bush: The KING of YouTube: Mr. Beast thread (2.4M impressions, 7,294 likes)
excerpt: "The KING of Youtube: Mr. Beast. Over the last 12 months, he's gained over 50,000,000 subscribers. So I binge-watched 100 hours of his videos to study how he's done it so quickly. Here's his 3-part framework for rapid growth (that you can use on any platform)."

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a framework (and the author's newsletter) to creators who want growth on the promise of Mr. Beast's method because the author did 100 hours of study and the subject gained 50 million subscribers in a year.
structure.hook: Bold claim plus a time-bound big number
structure.close: framework delivered in thread; newsletter link
structure.voice_notes: Short lines, numbers, one promise sentence packing what, why, who.

results.detail: Author-stated final stats: 2,400,502 impressions, 7,294 likes, 1,382 retweets, 171 replies, 1,000+ new email subscribers; introduction says it helped lock in 5,000 followers. The hooks guide also credits the hook's striking image.

lessons: Hook formula: moment in time, big specific number, credibility from stated effort, one-sentence promise with who/what/why.
Author-reported metrics with a newsletter conversion count: the rare organic record with a downstream result.
notes: Hook text taken from the Ship 30 hooks article (Example 4); metrics from the viral-threads article. Dickie Bush's site lists the thread title '3 Lessons Learned Studying The King of YouTube'.

title: Unnamed X thread: If you're a man in your 20s / Read this: (50,000+ likes)
author_or_company: unknown (shown in Ship 30 for 30 hooks guide)
excerpt: "If you're a man in your 20s" / "Read this:"

structure.argument_sentence: This sells attention (and the thread's advice) to men in their twenties on the promise that what follows is for them specifically because the hook filters by identity and withholds everything else.
structure.hook: Exact audience call-out plus two-word imperative
structure.voice_notes: Minimal; curiosity gap by omission.

results.detail: Ship 30 states the thread earned over 50,000 likes; author not named on the page.

lessons: Call-out and disqualifier in the first line (YouTube 0-5s rule applied to text).
Describes the reader's attribute, which the Meta spec forbids for ads; fine for organic.
notes: Author unknown; metric is third-party reported.

title: Ship 30 for 30: College completely failed in teaching me how to write (X thread)
author_or_company: Ship 30 for 30 author (Dickie Bush or Nicolas Cole; page written first person)
excerpt: "College completely failed in teaching me how to write. So I spent over 500 hours studying legendary authors and copywriters. But unlike college, these won't cost you $120,000. Here they are for free."

structure.argument_sentence: This sells writing lessons (and the authors' program) to people who feel college did not teach them to write on the promise of the real curriculum free because the author put in 500 hours and contrasts $0 with $120,000.
structure.hook: Silent controversial opinion the reader already holds
structure.big_idea: The writing education college owed you, free
structure.voice_notes: Four beats: opinion, credibility, contrast, delivery.

results.detail: Author states the cost-comparison line "gives the free insights far more perceived value" and "drove most of the thread's success"; no numeric metrics given on the page.

lessons: Price anchor works in organic: contrast the free thing against the expensive alternative in one line.
'Twist the knife' beat: credibility then contrast.
notes: No numbers; included for the annotated hook structure.

title: Nicolas Cole: Over the past 10 years I have read over 500 business books (X thread)
author_or_company: Nicolas Cole (@Nicolascole77), shown in Ship 30 for 30 hooks guide
excerpt: "Over the past 10 years... I have read over 500 business books. 99% (of these business books) were 1 idea stretched across 300 pages. Save yourself the time. Read these 10 ↓"

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a reading list to busy business readers on the promise of skipping 490 padded books because the author read them all and says what everyone suspects.
structure.hook: Time-based opener plus a credibility count
structure.mechanism: curation by someone who did the reading
structure.big_idea: Most business books are one idea; here are the ten that aren't
structure.voice_notes: Confessional count, blunt verdict, directional CTA.

results.detail: No metrics stated on the page; annotated as a model hook by Ship 30.

lessons: Credibility stated as a number of hours or books, never as a title.
CTA as verb, object, location ('Read these 10 ↓').
notes: Structure-only record.

title: Justin Welsh: Remember the good old days? (LinkedIn, May 2025)
excerpt: Hook: "Remember the good old days?" (body not reproduced).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells Welsh's worldview (and newsletter) to overworked professionals on the promise that a simpler life is available because the opener taps shared nostalgia before the argument.
structure.hook: Shared-sentiment question
structure.voice_notes: Four words, question, emotional recall; Welsh posts daily with an image and adds the link after publishing (Josh Spector).

results.detail: Ranked #1 of the top 50 LinkedIn hooks for the two weeks before May 17, 2025 by a third-party tool with an undefined 'Popularity' score of 2604.19; no reactions, comments or impressions stated. Welsh's account-level figures per Josh Spector: 471,000 LinkedIn followers, '$5 million solopreneur business', one post per day.

lessons: The shortest hook in the top 50 is a question that names a feeling, not a benefit.
Third-party popularity scores are not results; keep type 'none'.
notes: Welsh had 8 of the top 50 hooks in the list (also: "You can just do things.", "Most people are stuck.", "I burned out chasing perfection.", "You don't need permission.").

title: Samridhi Bhardwaj: This 2-second positioning shift helped our client land an $80K deal (LinkedIn, May 2025)
funnel_position: lead generation for a positioning service
excerpt: Hook: "This 2-second positioning shift helped our client land an $80K deal." (body not reproduced).

structure.argument_sentence: This sells positioning consulting to founders on the promise of bigger deals because one small change produced a specific $80K result for a client.
structure.hook: Tiny input, specific dollar output
structure.voice_notes: Case-study hook with a number; sales intent inside the story.

results.detail: Ranked #6 of 50 by third-party 'Popularity' score 615.65; no engagement figures stated.

lessons: Organic sales post pattern: client result with a dollar figure in line one; the standard requires that figure to carry a ledger ID.
notes: Result claim is the author's; unverified.

title: Nathan Apodaca (@420doggface208): skateboarding to 'Dreams' with Ocean Spray (TikTok, September 2020)
excerpt: After his truck broke down, Apodaca filmed himself skateboarding down a highway to work drinking Ocean Spray cran-raspberry juice and lip-syncing Fleetwood Mac's "Dreams" (no caption captured).

structure.argument_sentence: This sold nothing on purpose; it moved juice and a 43-year-old song by showing an ordinary man content in a moment, product in hand.
structure.hook: POV motion, music, calm face
structure.voice_notes: No words spoken; product visible throughout.

results.detail: Over 50 million views worldwide (Wikipedia, ref. 160). "Dreams" reached No. 1 on Billboard Rock Digital Song Sales in October 2020 and re-entered the Hot 100 at No. 21 (Oct 17, 2020), rising to No. 12; Top 50 most-streamed on Spotify and Apple Music in US, UK, Australia, NZ. Ocean Spray gave Apodaca a new truck. No Ocean Spray sales figures in fetched sources.

lessons: Real person on camera, proposition (mood) in the first second, product shown not described: the Reels spec in its purest form.
Downstream result documented for the song, not the brand; record what is actually measured.
notes: Organic UGC, not an ad; included as the TikTok control the paid format imitates.

title: Hyram Yarbro: CeraVe recommendations (TikTok/YouTube, March-October 2020)
funnel_position: none at the time (later paid partnership)
excerpt: Skincare creator reviewing and recommending CeraVe products in short videos (video text not captured by sources).

structure.argument_sentence: This sold a drugstore moisturizer to skincare-obsessed teens on the promise that the cheap dermatologist brand beats the expensive ones because an independent reviewer with ingredient knowledge said so.
structure.hook: Independent expert verdict on a cheap product
structure.big_idea: The $15 bottle the experts actually use
structure.voice_notes: Reviewer register; candor about brands he dislikes.

results.detail: Wikipedia: videos "reportedly led to an 89% increase in its global sales in 2020" (Ozuem & Willis 2022, Palgrave; i-D, Aug 3, 2020); about $3.2 million in media impact value (WWD, Dec 7, 2020). Led to a paid L'Oréal partnership (Allure, June 3, 2021). Attribution is reported, not proven.

lessons: Third-party authority plus mechanism (ingredients) sells a stage-4 category without the brand speaking.
Record 'reportedly' attributions as such.
notes: Cross-checked with https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyram_Yarbro (same figures).

title: Stanley Quencher: The Buy Guide influencer push (2017-2020) and TikTok growth
author_or_company: The Buy Guide (Ashlee LeSueur) and TikTok creators; Stanley 1913
excerpt: A women-run Utah blog found the Quencher at Bed Bath & Beyond in 2017, gave it to friends and recommended it to followers; Stanley agreed to let them sell 5,000 units directly (post text not captured).

structure.argument_sentence: This sold a discontinued-in-waiting tumbler to women on the promise of a cup that fits the car and keeps ice all day because trusted peers showed it in daily life.
structure.hook: Peer recommendation, product in hand
structure.voice_notes: Lifestyle, color-drop urgency.

results.detail: Wikipedia: The Buy Guide sold 5,000 Quenchers, after which Stanley resumed production; Quencher sales rose 275% from 2020 to 2021 (NYT Jan 5, 2024; Seattle Times Jan 12, 2024); Stanley annual sales about $70 million in 2019 and an estimated $750 million in 2023 (CNBC Dec 23, 2023), attributed primarily to the Quencher.

losing_variants.description: Stanley's own prior marketing of the Quencher to its traditional male outdoor audience
losing_variants.result: Product was slated for discontinuation before the influencer push, per source

lessons: Same product, new market: the market decision outranked every copy decision.
Influencer demonstration in daily use is the proof type for a commodity object.
notes: The November 2023 car-fire TikTok was not covered in the fetched source and is omitted.

title: Google Ads responsive search ads: official performance figures and pinning example
excerpt: Example pinned headlines: "Official Website" and "The Official Site" (both competing for Headline position 1). Fifteen headlines of 30 characters and four descriptions of 90 characters per RSA.

structure.argument_sentence: This records Google's own stated aggregates for RSA construction rather than a single ad: more distinct assets and higher Ad Strength yield more conversions at similar cost.
structure.hook: n/a
structure.voice_notes: n/a

results.detail: Google internal data (Aug 15-20, 2025): improving Ad Strength from Poor to Excellent, advertisers "find 15% more clicks & conversions on average"; going from one to two RSAs in an ad group, "a 6.6% increase in conversions at a similar cost per conversion on average"; two to three RSAs, "an average 3.7% increase in conversions."

losing_variants.description: Pinning two headlines to the same position
losing_variants.result: Reduces combinations; Google's example shows ads then alternate only those two

lessons: Supports the spec's 15 distinct headline shapes: asset diversity (Ad Strength) is the measured lever.
Vendor aggregate, not a copy control; no example RSA with CTR data was found in fetched sources.
notes: Placeholder for the RSA category; see gaps.

title: Dickie Bush: first LinkedIn post, ~500k views and 4,500 likes
excerpt: Post text shown only as a screenshot on the source; not captured. Taught structure: lead-in (attention plus payoff), main points, CTA; about five lines before 'see more'; links in the first comment.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells writing habits (and Ship 30) to LinkedIn professionals on the promise of practical, aspirational advice because the post is actionable within minutes and the author's results are visible.
structure.hook: unknown (screenshot)
structure.close: question or takeaway prompt; link in first comment
structure.voice_notes: Short sentences, line breaks, one sentence then three bullets pattern.

results.detail: Ship 30 states the first LinkedIn post reached about 500k views and 4,500 likes with no existing LinkedIn following. Separately, the Twitter guide reports a Dickie Bush thread reaching about 5M views when the account had roughly 9,000 followers, and the ultimate guide cites 4.6 million people reached from a tweet at ~20,000 followers.

lessons: Organic social spec confirmed by a practitioner with numbers: five lines to earn 'see more', lead-in / points / CTA, link in a comment.
Ship 30 explicitly advises against the Twitter-style recap on LinkedIn.
notes: Excerpt unavailable; structure rules recorded.
